title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Milwaukee, WI: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Milwaukee welders, fitters and QC staff: Parts A, B and C, code book choice, online study or on-site at your plant.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Milwaukee, Wisconsin: A Six-Day Course for Machinery, Pressure and Structural Welding Inspectors
html:
Milwaukee builds heavy things out of welded steel: mining machines, water heaters and boilers, engines, frames, castings and the structural steel that holds up the plants that make them. That work keeps a steady demand for people who can read a welding symbol, measure a fillet and judge a weld against a code. This page is for welders, fitters, QC staff and engineers in the Milwaukee area who want to sit the American Welding Society (AWS) Certified Welding Inspector examination, and for the managers who want several of their people ready for it. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day (6-day) CWI exam-preparation course. The exam itself belongs to AWS: the society runs all three parts, scores them and issues the certificate, and Atlantis's part is the preparation. To scope it, ask for a Milwaukee CWI exam prep quote.

What the course is, in one paragraph

It is six days of structured preparation for the three parts of the AWS CWI exam: Fundamentals (Part A), the hands-on Practical (Part B) and Code Application (Part C). A candidate working alone gets a paced plan, reading material and a bank of practice items to work through online, plus a named instructor to message when a symbol or table will not make sense. A company can instead bring the six days to its own plant for a group. Nothing is timetabled, and Atlantis has no classroom in Wisconsin. Every practice item is drafted in-house against the subject list AWS publishes; none comes from a real examination. AWS has not approved or endorsed the course, and no one at Atlantis sees the exam or your score. The day-by-day outline is on the AWS CWI exam prep course page.

Milwaukee's welding economy: machines, pressure equipment and lake shipyards

Southeast Wisconsin is one of the densest manufacturing regions in the Midwest, and much of that manufacturing is welded. Three groups of work drive most of the inspection demand.

Mining, construction and industrial machinery

Komatsu's mining equipment business has its US base on the Harbor District lakefront in Milwaukee, and the region has a long history of building shovels, draglines, cranes and other machines whose booms, frames and buckets are thick plate welded with flux cored and submerged arc processes. Joints on this kind of equipment are large, multi-pass and highly restrained. The defects that matter are lack of fusion between passes, toe cracks at the end of stiffeners and hydrogen cracking in thick sections that were not preheated. An inspector on that floor spends the day checking preheat, interpass temperature, fit-up and weld size, which is exactly the vocabulary of Part A and Part B.

Water heaters, boilers and pressure equipment

A. O. Smith, the water heater and boiler manufacturer, is headquartered in the Milwaukee area, and the wider region supplies tanks, heat exchangers and pressure parts. Pressure work runs to ASME rules: welding procedures and welder qualifications under ASME Section IX, and construction under the relevant section of the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. A CWI in a pressure-equipment shop reviews procedure qualification records, checks that a welder's qualification covers the position and thickness on the job, and controls weld visual acceptance before the part goes to NDT or a hydrostatic test.

Shipyards on Lake Michigan

Wisconsin's two big Great Lakes shipyards sit a couple of hours north of the city, Fincantieri Marinette Marine in Marinette and Fincantieri Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay. Naval work follows Navy welding and inspection documents, so a CWI is often one qualification among several on a ship program, but the skills transfer directly: joint fit-up, distortion control, visual acceptance and record keeping. Some Milwaukee welders commute to yard work for a season, and the CWI travels with them.

Around those three groups sits a long tail of job shops, foundries that repair castings by welding, trailer and truck-body builders, food and dairy equipment makers working in stainless steel, and steel fabricators supplying new plants, warehouses and the lakefront redevelopment. Each needs someone who can say yes or no to a weld with confidence.

Who hires CWIs around Milwaukee, and why

  • Original equipment manufacturers. Customers and dealers want weld quality documented, and a CWI on the quality team gives the plant a recognized person to sign visual acceptance and supervise welder testing.
  • Structural steel fabricators and erectors. Shops supplying buildings and bridges in Wisconsin and northern Illinois work to AWS D1.1 for buildings and AWS D1.5 for bridges. Fabricator certification programs and project specifications expect qualified inspection personnel, and owners commonly name the CWI.
  • Inspection and testing firms. Third-party inspectors cover building projects, utility work and supplier audits. A CWI is the usual entry ticket for the welding side of that work.
  • Utilities and power plants. Outage work on boilers and piping brings contract welders and a need for welding inspection to ASME B31.1 and owner specifications.
  • Contractors on public works. Bridge rehabilitation on the freeway system, including steel spans such as the Hoan Bridge on Interstate 794, brings field welding and repair welding that the state and its consultants inspect.

A practical point for production people: in many Milwaukee plants the person already accepting welds informally is a senior welder or lead hand. The CWI turns that judgment into a credential a customer or auditor recognizes, and it moves with you if you change employers.

Which code book Milwaukee candidates tend to choose for Part C

Part C is open book, and you choose the code. AWS lists several options, including AWS D1.1 (structural steel), API 1104 (pipelines), AWS D1.2 (aluminum), AWS D1.5 (bridges), AWS D15.1 (railroad cars and locomotives), AWS D17.1 (aerospace fusion welding) and an ASME option built on Section IX with the B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes. Check the editions AWS names when you apply, because the exam edition can trail the newest one in print. Background reading: AWS D1.1 and the D1.1 visual acceptance guide.

Your Milwaukee-area workCode most candidates pickWhy
Machinery frames, booms, structural fabricationAWS D1.1Most heavy equipment and building steel is specified to D1.1 or a customer standard built on it.
Boilers, tanks, process and power pipingASME Section IX with B31.1 / B31.3Matches the procedure and welder qualification rules you already work under.
Bridge girders and highway steelAWS D1.5The bridge code has its own fracture-critical and inspection provisions.
Aluminum boats, enclosures and framesAWS D1.2Aluminum acceptance and qualification differ from steel in ways the exam tests.

The course works in whichever book you choose. On-site groups can split by code if a plant has both structural and pressure work.

The AWS Milwaukee Section

AWS organizes its members into local sections grouped by district. Milwaukee has its own section, part of AWS District 12. A local section is where welding engineers, inspectors, instructors, suppliers and students meet, hear technical talks and support scholarships. For a CWI candidate the section is worth joining for two reasons: you meet working inspectors who will tell you what the job is actually like in local shops, and you hear about employers looking for qualified people before the jobs are posted. Section meetings are also a good place to find someone who can verify your welding-related experience, which AWS asks for on the application. Look up current officers and meeting details through the sections directory on aws.org.

Welding programs in the Milwaukee area

Most CWIs start as welders, and the experience years on the AWS eligibility table are easier to document when they begin with formal training. Milwaukee Area Technical College offers a Welding Technology associate degree, taught in person at its Downtown Milwaukee, Mequon, Oak Creek and Walker's Square locations, with a schedule that the state's training provider list describes as roughly thirty hours a week over about sixty-four weeks. Other technical colleges in southeast Wisconsin also run welding diplomas and short certificates. An associate degree in welding counts toward the education side of the AWS eligibility table, which lowers the years of experience you need, so check how your own diploma or degree is classed before you apply.

Graduates who move into inspection often find the welding symbols and code-reading parts of the exam harder than the metallurgy. Production training teaches you to make a weld; the exam asks you to read a drawing, find a table and justify acceptance in writing. Those are the areas the six days lean on.

Sitting the AWS exam from Milwaukee

The exam is split by format. Parts A and C are computer-based tests that you book at a Prometric center once AWS sends your confirmation letter with an eligibility code. AWS says Prometric operates more than one hundred centers in the United States, so most Milwaukee candidates can sit A and C within driving distance; use the Prometric locator to find the nearest one. Part B, the practical, is different. AWS runs it itself at its seminar and examination locations on fixed dates, and the application deadline for Part B falls several weeks before the exam date. That may mean a trip, so check the AWS seminar and examination schedule on aws.org before you commit to a month.

The rules worth knowing before you plan: Part A has 150 questions; Part B combines hands-on activities with AWS-supplied tools and specimens and 46 related questions; Part C is open book with roughly 50 to 65 questions; and AWS requires at least 72% on each part. Each computer-based part allows up to two hours of exam time. AWS publishes its current exam and seminar fees on its website; for budgeting, use the CWI exam budget planner.

How the six days fit a Milwaukee candidate

Studying on your own around shifts

Many candidates here work first or second shift in a plant, and some work overtime during peak season. The online route lets you spread the six days of material across evenings and weekends. A sensible rhythm is to finish the Fundamentals blocks first, because welding symbols and terminology run through every part, then work the code book alongside your normal job so that the tables become familiar, and save the timed practice papers for the last two weeks before your Prometric appointment. You can send questions to the instructor as you go, so a confusing symbol or table does not sit unanswered for a week.

Six days at your plant

For an employer with several candidates, the six days can be delivered at your facility. That changes the practical preparation most. Instead of generic exercises, the group measures welds from your own production with your own fillet gauges, bridge cam gauges and undercut gauges, and compares them with the acceptance criteria in your customer's specification. Code practice can run in the book your shop works to. It also removes travel and keeps the group together for the timed practice day. The plant cannot apply on anyone's behalf: every candidate files with AWS in their own name, clears the experience and eyesight rules alone and books a personal exam slot.

Eligibility checkpoints before you start studying

  1. Experience. AWS ties the years of welding-related work you need to your education: five years with a high school diploma, fewer with a welding degree or technical coursework, more with less schooling. Write down employers, dates, codes and duties now, with a contact who can confirm each job.
  2. Vision. AWS requires a vision examination on its own form, covering near vision and color perception, performed by a qualified eye-care or medical professional within the window AWS sets. Glasses for close work are fine.
  3. Code choice. Decide your Part C book before you study, not after.
  4. Timing. Work back from a Part B date you can actually attend, then book A and C with Prometric.

If your experience falls short of the CWI threshold, AWS also offers the Certified Associate Welding Inspector, which works under a CWI's supervision. The CWI requirements guide walks through both.

After the CWI: where Milwaukee inspectors go next

AWS treats the CWI as a nine-year credential and expects a renewal filing at the three-year and six-year marks. Within that span, Milwaukee inspectors tend to branch in one of three directions. Some move into supplier quality and audit customers' and vendors' welding programs. Some add nondestructive testing, because a CWI who can also perform magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing is more useful on a machinery floor; under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies NDT personnel after method training and experience, and Atlantis provides that training (see NDT training for Milwaukee and VT Level 2 training). Others move toward the Senior CWI once they run an inspection program. For what local NDT work looks like, see magnetic particle testing in Milwaukee and ultrasonic testing in Milwaukee.

Atlantis offers API 510, 570 and 653 exam prep as separate self-paced online courses; candidates interested in in-service inspection can read about those certifications on api.org.

Nearby CWI prep pages and what to send for a quote

Candidates from the wider Great Lakes region often compare notes across cities. See CWI exam prep for Chicago, Minneapolis and Detroit.

For a quote, say how many people need preparing, give a line or two on each person's schooling and years at the torch, name the Part C book they lean toward, and, if the six days should come to you, tell us the plant's location and what inspection gauges and scrap welds are on hand. Use the Milwaukee enquiry link and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is there a CWI prep class I can attend in person in Milwaukee?
faq.a: Atlantis does not run a public classroom in Milwaukee. A lone candidate works the six-day material online and messages an instructor with questions; a company with several candidates can host the six days at its Wisconsin site instead. See the course outline.

The American Welding Society. AWS sets eligibility, administers all three parts of the exam and issues the certificate. The Atlantis course prepares you; it does not certify anyone and is not approved or endorsed by AWS.

faq.q: Where do Milwaukee candidates take the CWI exam?
faq.a: Parts A and C are computer-based at a Prometric center, and AWS says there are more than one hundred in the US. Part B, the practical, is run by AWS at its own seminar and exam locations on fixed dates, so check the AWS schedule for the nearest site.

faq.q: Which code book should a Milwaukee machinery or structural welder choose?
faq.a: Most pick AWS D1.1, because structural steel and most heavy equipment frames are specified to it. Pressure-equipment staff often pick the ASME Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3 option. Read more on AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Does a Welding Technology degree from MATC reduce the experience I need?
faq.a: An associate degree in welding sits on the education side of the AWS eligibility table and lowers the years of welding-related experience required. Confirm how AWS classes your specific diploma or degree before you apply.

faq.q: What score do I need on each part?
faq.a: AWS lists a minimum of 72% on each of Parts A, B and C. Part A has 150 questions, Part B adds 46 questions to its hands-on tasks, and Part C has roughly 50 to 65 open-book questions.

faq.q: Can our plant have the six days delivered on site?
faq.a: Yes. When the course comes to a Wisconsin plant, the group practises on welds cut from its own production with the gauges its inspectors already carry. Applications to AWS stay personal. Request a quote.

faq.q: Is it worth adding NDT training after the CWI?
faq.a: On a machinery floor a CWI who can also run magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing covers more of the inspection plan. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies NDT staff after training and experience. See NDT training for Milwaukee.

faq.q: Are the practice questions real AWS exam questions?
faq.a: No. Each item is drafted from scratch against the subject list in the AWS body of knowledge, and nobody at Atlantis can see the live exam or its item bank. Free method practice tests are also on the NDT practice tests page.

faq.q: How long does the CWI certification last?
faq.a: Nine years in total, by the AWS rules, with a renewal filing at year three and again at year six. At the nine-year point you recertify, for example by retaking Part B or by logging professional development hours.
